fixture.scope: Bounded direct/journal load and transaction-size measurements under CPU/RAM caps.
fixture.methodology: Fresh private volumes and identical cached PostgreSQL/core/pgduck/storage images in every mode. Both paths use the same text-valued events and current apply_change_run functions. One warmup transaction (one seed row per table) is published before measurement; it is excluded from publication counts and object traces. Direct worker persists across all measured transactions and uses bounded 1-second/32-transaction coalescing and uses a loopback superuser. Journal uses the existing managed supervisor, unprivileged worker, source schema validation and protocol streaming; a test-only next_batch wrapper caps publications at 1 for the matched control or 32 for the coalesced reference. Original journal admission, publication, generation fencing and recovery functions remain unchanged. This compares the implementations, not just the isolated cost of journal durability: worker lifecycle, privileges, metadata checks and protocol differ. Coalesced reference uses a 1-second interval and INSERT grouping. Two-second resource/progress observers are identical; CPU includes observer processes in database/engine containers, excludes host/controller/MinIO. Publication delay is a sampled upper bound. No competing local qualification, no cache clearing, no production capacity or significance claim. This cohort uses one CPU/512 MiB for PostgreSQL and one CPU/2 GiB for pgduck (1536-MB engine query limit). Postgres-user observers read database/engine process memory; a separate root observer adds the root-owned direct worker without requiring ptrace capabilities. All modes run both observers. Worker exit diagnostics record its lifetime RSS peak and CPU, including warmup. memory.peak includes fixture startup and page cache; it is not process RSS. Sustained phase has paced mixed transactions; memory phase has one large INSERT transaction and no offered pacing. Memory payloads use per-row MD5 strings with varied blocks. Samples are every two seconds and can miss short peaks; cgroup lifetime peak and worker VmHWM supplement samples. Expanded profile disables swap; both RAM and swap limits are recorded. Logical decoding work memory is 64 KiB in both modes, so larger transactions stream without the immediate debug setting. No concurrent qualification runs.

fixture.scope: Bounded direct/journal load and transaction-size measurements under CPU/RAM caps.
fixture.methodology: Fresh private volumes and identical cached PostgreSQL/core/pgduck/storage images in every mode. Both paths use the same text-valued events and current apply_change_run functions. One warmup transaction (one seed row per table) is published before measurement; it is excluded from publication counts and object traces. Direct worker persists across all measured transactions and uses bounded 1-second/32-transaction coalescing and uses a loopback superuser. Journal uses the existing managed supervisor, unprivileged worker, source schema validation and protocol streaming; a test-only next_batch wrapper caps publications at 1 for the matched control or 32 for the coalesced reference. Original journal admission, publication, generation fencing and recovery functions remain unchanged. This compares the implementations, not just the isolated cost of journal durability: worker lifecycle, privileges, metadata checks and protocol differ. Coalesced reference uses a 1-second interval and INSERT grouping. Two-second resource/progress observers are identical; CPU includes observer processes in database/engine containers, excludes host/controller/MinIO. Publication delay is a sampled upper bound. No competing local qualification, no cache clearing, no production capacity or significance claim. This cohort uses one CPU/512 MiB for PostgreSQL and one CPU/1 GiB for pgduck (768-MB engine query limit). Postgres-user observers read database/engine process memory; a separate root observer adds the root-owned direct worker without requiring ptrace capabilities. All modes run both observers. Worker exit diagnostics record its lifetime RSS peak and CPU, including warmup. memory.peak includes fixture startup and page cache; it is not process RSS. Sustained phase has paced mixed transactions; memory phase has one large INSERT transaction and no offered pacing. Memory payloads use per-row MD5 strings with varied blocks. Samples are every two seconds and can miss short peaks; cgroup lifetime peak and worker VmHWM supplement samples. No concurrent qualification runs.

caveats: One trial per size/mode; no statistical or maximum-capacity claim.
Final memory cohort explicitly disables swap; older smoke/load discovery cohorts did not constrain swap.

Load discovery used the older maximum-published-XID observer. Its completion counts are upper bounds. Both failed the 90-second drain deadline, so these runs demonstrate overload but are excluded from CPU-saving comparisons.
The earlier overload cohort also reported a final-hash error when neither fixture passed; no successful hash comparison existed. The harness now skips empty comparison groups.

Earlier large-transaction journal timing/hash assertions were invalid because bookkeeping transactions could satisfy the old frontier. The final cohort uses exact application XIDs and excludes empty bookkeeping from batch counts.
Worker lifetime RSS/CPU includes warmup; worker CPU is already part of PostgreSQL cgroup CPU.
Cgroup peaks include startup, cache and observer processes, and are not process RSS.
next_gate: Profile publication cost as mirror/file metadata grows, then implement measured memory admission and repeat sustained workload at a defined deployment envelope.
